question: A researcher is scanning a Claude-written sector briefing for signs that something in it has been fabricated. Which two features are the strongest warning signs? Select two.
options: A) A named industry report with a specific year that cannot be located anywhere at all.
B) Technical vocabulary from the sector used throughout the briefing without definitions.
C) Two figures in the same briefing that cannot both be true as they are written there.
D) A response noticeably longer than the researcher expected for a briefing of this kind.
E) Cautious phrasing such as "it appears that" appearing in several of the paragraphs.
correct_answers: A) A named industry report with a specific year that cannot be located anywhere at all.
C) Two figures in the same briefing that cannot both be true as they are written there.
explanations: Correct. A confidently named source that does not exist is the classic fabrication signature, and the specificity of the citation is what makes it convincing.
Sector vocabulary is what a briefing would naturally contain. It affects readability for a lay audience but carries no information about truthfulness.
Correct. Internal contradiction is independent evidence: at least one of the two figures must be wrong, and it is detectable from the text alone with no external source.
Length reflects how the request was framed. Long answers are not more likely to be invented than short ones, so this is not a useful signal by itself.
Hedging language signals uncertainty rather than fabrication. If anything, unhedged confidence about a specific unverifiable fact is the more worrying pattern.
